title: From Transformation to Target State: Rethinking Query Representation for Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval

paper.title: From Transformation to Target State: Rethinking Query Representation for Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval
paper.abstract: Abstract Composed image retrieval (CIR) aims to retrieve a desired target image from a query consisting of a reference image and a modification text. This task exhibits an unusual representational asymmetry: the modification text specifies a transition from the reference state, whereas retrieval candidates depict completed target states. This creates a representation mismatch for zero-shot methods that query pretrained vision-language spaces directly with transformation-oriented language. We study this mismatch and reformulate zero-shot composed image retrieval as target-state reconstruction followed by retrieval. We instantiate this formulation with ASAP-CIR , a training-free framework that reconstructs a static target representation using a frozen multimodal large language model (MLLM). The representation combines multiple holistic descriptions with a variable set of importance-weighted atomic semantics, thereby preserving both overall target identity and fine-grained visual constraints. Retrieval then integrates holistic state alignment, atomic constraint grounding, and calibrated target-state evidence aggregation. A controlled text-only diagnostic shows that target-side static query formulations achieve more reliable retrieval than dynamic composed query formulations, particularly when source-state semantics must be suppressed or transformed. Experiments on FashionIQ, CIRR, and CIRCO further characterize the effectiveness and limitations of this representation principle, with the clearest gains on the multi-target CIRCO benchmark. These results show that how composed intent is represented before retrieval is a consequential design choice, distinct from the choice of retrieval backbone itself.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Composed image retrieval (CIR) enables users to search for a desired image through a visual reference and natural-language feedback. Unlike conventional text-to-image retrieval, however, CIR does not directly provide a description of the target. It provides evidence about a reference state together with an instruction that specifies how this state should change. The retrieval system must infer the completed target state before it can compare the query with candidate images. This capability supports interactive product search, fashion recommendation, visual editing assistance, and open-domain image search, but also makes CIR fundamentally different from ordinary image-text matching. Existing CIR methods can be roughly grouped into supervised and zero-shot paradigms. Supervised methods learn image-text composition from annotated triplets and can achieve strong performance when sufficient training data are available ( Vo et al., 2019 ; Baldrati et al., 2022 ; Han et al., 2023 ; Song et al., 2024 ) . Collecting such triplets is expensive, however, and models trained on fixed datasets may not generalize to new domains or unseen user intents. Zero-shot CIR (ZS-CIR) instead reuses pretrained vision-language models (VLMs), especially Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP), or employs large language models (LLMs) and multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to infer target-related text ( Saito et al., 2023 ; Baldrati et al., 2023 ; Karthik et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Tang et al., 2025 ) . Although this removes task-specific training, it exposes a more fundamental issue: the input semantics describe a transition, while the retrieval space is organized around observable visual states. We refer to this issue as the representation mismatch in ZS-CIR. A modification such as “remove the person”, “make the bottle orange”, or “add a wooden log” denotes an operation rather than a completed visual state. Directly encoding such language may preserve removed entities, superseded attributes, or editing predicates that should not be visible in the target. The difficulty is therefore not merely to compose an image and a sentence; it is to represent the intended target state in a pretrained image-text space that was not explicitly trained to execute state transitions. Our central insight is to reconstruct the target state before retrieval instead of asking a pretrained VLM to perform an implicit state transition inside its embedding space. Target-state reconstruction canonicalizes diverse dynamic instructions into static descriptions of what should be visible. Yet one caption is not sufficient for every composed query. The intended state has complementary holistic and atomic structure: holistic descriptions preserve target identity and scene coherence, whereas atomic semantics retain changed attributes, counts, relations, and newly introduced objects as explicit visual constraints. We therefore represent the reconstructed state as a static target representation containing both levels. MLLM reasoning remains restricted to the query side, while candidate features can be precomputed for efficient retrieval. Figure 1: Motivation of ASAP-CIR. The left panels compare three query formulation paradigms: (a) pseudo-word inversion directly combines an inverted visual token with dynamic modification text; (b) MLLM-based reasoning generates a target description without explicitly constraining it to static visual semantics; and (c) ASAP-CIR reconstructs the composed query as complementary holistic descriptions and importance-weighted atomic semantics for multi-level retrieval. Panel (d) visualizes the phenomenon observed in our diagnostic experiments: target-side static query embeddings are more closely aligned with the target embedding region, whereas dynamic composed query embeddings are more dispersed and frequently deviate from the intended target state. We instantiate this formulation with ASAP-CIR. ASAP abbreviates A tomic S tatic sem A ntic P arsing, and ASAP-CIR is a training-free framework for ZS-CIR. As illustrated on the left of Fig. 1 , a frozen MLLM reconstructs each dynamic query as a static target representation composed of multiple holistic descriptions and importance-weighted atomic semantics. The holistic descriptions capture target identity and scene-level coherence; the atomic semantics expose objects, attributes, relations, counts, styles, and scene cues as explicit retrieval constraints. Candidate images are ranked using holistic state alignment and atomic constraint grounding, followed by calibrated target-state evidence aggregation. The right panel summarizes the diagnostic evidence motivating this design: target-side static query representations tend to occupy the target-aligned region of CLIP’s feature space more consistently than dynamic composed query representations. To examine whether this reformulation is supported by the behavior of pretrained vision-language representations, we further conduct a controlled text-only diagnostic study. Under this protocol, static target descriptions retrieve the intended target descriptions more reliably than formulations that combine a reference description and modification instruction. This result does not imply a universal inability of CLIP to encode dynamic language; instead, it shows that query formulation materially affects retrieval alignment in the considered CIR setting. Benchmark experiments further reveal that the benefit is dataset dependent: it is most pronounced on CIRCO, while FashionIQ and CIRR expose limitations in fine-grained garment discrimination and deeper candidate ranking. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: • We identify and formulate a representation mismatch in ZS-CIR: transformation-oriented instructions are used to query pretrained image-text spaces whose candidates express completed visual states. We consequently reformulate ZS-CIR as target-state reconstruction followed by retrieval. • We introduce a multi-level static target representation that jointly preserves holistic semantics and fine-grained atomic constraints. ASAP-CIR provides a training-free realization of this principle and a structured interface between frozen MLLM reasoning and pretrained VLM retrieval. • We establish controlled evidence that target-state formulations are better aligned with pretrained CLIP representations for several transformation types, and evaluate the resulting retrieval behavior on FashionIQ, CIRR, and CIRCO, including its benefits and remaining boundaries.

sections.heading: 2.1 Composed Image Retrieval
sections.text: Composed image retrieval retrieves images according to a reference image and a natural-language modification. Unlike conventional image retrieval, in which a query is expressed through a single modality, CIR requires the retrieval model to preserve query-relevant visual content from the reference while satisfying the changes expressed in language. Existing CIR methods can be broadly divided into supervised and zero-shot paradigms. Supervised methods learn this composition from annotated triplets of reference images, modification texts, and target images. Early approaches such as TIRG ( Vo et al., 2019 ) learn dedicated feature composition modules to combine visual and textual cues, while later methods further exploit pretrained vision-language models, cross-modal attention, or task-specific pretraining objectives to improve composed retrieval performance ( Baldrati et al., 2022 ; Han et al., 2023 ; Song et al., 2024 ; Fu et al., 2026 ) . Although these methods achieve strong performance when training triplets are available, their reliance on annotated CIR data limits their scalability to new domains and retrieval scenarios. In addition, supervised models tend to inherit the semantic distribution of the training triplets, making it difficult to handle rare or open-ended modification intents without collecting new annotations. Several benchmarks have been proposed to support CIR research. Fashion200k ( Han et al., 2017 ) is an early fashion-domain benchmark that connects product images with relative textual feedback. FashionIQ ( Wu et al., 2021 ) further provides human-written natural language feedback for fashion retrieval across multiple garment categories. CIRR ( Liu et al., 2021 ) extends composed retrieval to real-life open-domain images and introduces both full-gallery and subset evaluation protocols, while CIRCO ( Baldrati et al., 2023 ) builds a challenging COCO-based benchmark with multiple valid target images for each query. To reduce the dependence on CIR triplets, recent studies have increasingly focused on ZS-CIR. One representative line of work follows the textual inversion paradigm. Pic2Word ( Saito et al., 2023 ) maps an input image into a pseudo-word token in the CLIP text embedding space, enabling the composed query to be represented as a text prompt. SEARLE ( Baldrati et al., 2023 ) improves this idea through a textual inversion mechanism that represents the reference image as a pseudo-word token and composes it with the relative caption. Subsequent methods such as LinCIR ( Gu et al., 2024 ) reduce the need for image-text supervision by using language-only training, while DeG ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , MOA ( Li et al., 2025 ) , and CoCo-IR ( Cao et al., 2026 ) further study data-efficient generalization, object-aware pseudo-word learning, and contextual composed retrieval. Beyond textual inversion, recent ZS-CIR methods also explore difference-aware composition, semantic flow, geodesic semantic expansion, and reward-guided test-time optimization, as represented by DiffComp, FlowCIR, G-MIXER, and TT-RLDR ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ; Lim et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) . These methods are elegant and efficient because they reuse or adapt the pretrained CLIP image-text alignment space. In textual inversion methods, however, the pseudo-word representation of the reference image is typically inserted into a prompt together with the original modification text. Consequently, explicit transition expressions such as removal, replacement, or attribute change may remain in the composed prompt and be passed directly to the CLIP text encoder. Such methods therefore implicitly assume that CLIP can interpret these dynamic modification semantics and combine them correctly with the pseudo-word representation. Another recent line of work explores training-free ZS-CIR with LLMs or MLLMs. CIReVL ( Karthik et al., 2024 ) first captions the reference image with a VLM and then uses an LLM to rewrite the composed query into target descriptions for CLIP retrieval. LDRE ( Yang et al., 2024 ) further generates dense reference captions and performs LLM-based divergent reasoning, followed by semantic-relevance-weighted caption ensemble. PrediCIR ( Tang et al., 2025 ) predicts missing target-relevant information with a world model, and CoTMR ( Sun et al., 2025 ) introduces chain-of-thought multi-scale reasoning for training-free retrieval. AutoCIR ( Cheng et al., 2025 ) formulates ZS-CIR as automatic multi-agent collaboration with planning, retrieval, and correction agents, while OSrCIR ( Tang et al., 2025 ) employs one-stage reflective chain-of-thought reasoning with an MLLM before retrieval. More recent methods such as STiTch ( Li et al., 2026 ) and WISER ( Wang et al., 2026 ) further improve training-free retrieval through semantic transition and transportation, wider search, deeper reasoning, or adaptive fusion. These approaches demonstrate that external reasoning can reduce reliance on directly encoding raw modification text. Because some of them infer descriptions of the target, their outputs may incidentally avoid explicit transition words and contain implicit static target semantics. However, static semantic formulation is generally a by-product rather than an explicit constraint: generated descriptions are not necessarily required to exclude source-state or transition-oriented expressions, nor are target requirements systematically organized at complementary semantic levels. Their primary emphasis is instead on composition, reasoning, search, or fusion. Accordingly, the distinction of ASAP-CIR is not merely the use of an MLLM or an additional patch-level matching branch. Existing methods mainly investigate how reference and modification information should be composed, reasoned over, or refined; our work instead asks how the inferred target state should be represented before retrieval. ASAP-CIR answers this question through a multi-level static target representation that combines holistic descriptions with importance-weighted atomic semantics, thereby making query representation itself an explicit component of retrieval design.

sections.heading: 2.2 Vision-Language Models for CIR
sections.text: Vision-language models (VLMs) have become a fundamental component of modern multimodal learning, as they provide a shared representation space for visual and textual information. Among them, CLIP, introduced by Radford et al. ( Radford et al., 2021 ) , is one of the most representative models for open-vocabulary visual understanding. CLIP is trained on large-scale image-text pairs using a contrastive learning objective, where matched image-text pairs are pulled closer and mismatched pairs are pushed apart in a shared embedding space. This simple yet scalable pretraining strategy enables CLIP to learn transferable visual representations and perform zero-shot recognition by comparing image features with natural language prompts. Due to its strong image-text alignment ability, CLIP has been widely adopted as a general-purpose backbone for many downstream tasks, including zero-shot and few-shot image classification, test-time adaptation, robust recognition, anomaly detection, image-language understanding, visual question answering, and compositional zero-shot learning ( Martin et al., 2024 ; Saha et al., 2024 ; Zanella and Ben Ayed, 2024 ; Ge et al., 2023 ; An et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2026 ; Jeong et al., 2023 ; Tschannen et al., 2023 ; Guo et al., 2023 ; Chen and Wu, 2024 ; Lu et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) . These studies demonstrate the broad transferability of pretrained vision-language representations. At the same time, they also suggest that the way a task is formulated in language can strongly affect how CLIP is used. This issue is particularly relevant to CIR, where the query text often specifies how one visual state should be transformed into another rather than simply describing a static image. In composed image retrieval, CLIP is particularly attractive because the task naturally requires matching visual content with language descriptions. Existing ZS-CIR methods often reuse CLIP as the core retrieval backbone, either by mapping the reference image into a pseudo-word token, generating target captions, or composing reference and modification semantics in the CLIP feature space ( Saito et al., 2023 ; Baldrati et al., 2023 ; Karthik et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) . Their success nevertheless depends on the ability of the pretrained text encoder to represent transformation-oriented language in a form suitable for matching completed visual states. This issue is relevant to negation, counting, relational changes, and object removal, where a query may mention concepts or attributes that should not appear in the target. In this work, we retain CLIP as the retrieval backbone but study whether reformulating the query as observable target-state semantics provides a more suitable retrieval representation under a controlled CIR protocol.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: This section presents ASAP-CIR as a concrete training-free solution to the query representation problem in zero-shot composed image retrieval (ZS-CIR). We use dynamic semantics to denote instructions that specify a transition from the reference state, and target-state semantics to denote visually observable content in the desired result. Motivated by the controlled evidence in Sec. 4.3 , ASAP-CIR follows a representation-centered pipeline: it reconstructs the intended target state from the composed query, expresses that state through complementary holistic descriptions and importance-weighted atomic semantics, and grounds both levels against candidate images. CLIP is therefore used primarily to align observable target-state semantics rather than to infer the transformation itself. Figure 2: Overview of the proposed ASAP-CIR framework. Given a composed query, the MLLM parser performs target-state semantic reconstruction and produces complementary holistic descriptions and importance-weighted atomic semantics. In the figure, these outputs are labeled “Holistic Descriptions” and “Weighted Atomic Semantics,” respectively. The holistic descriptions are encoded independently and combined by average pooling before being aligned with global image features to obtain the holistic evidence score. The atomic semantics are encoded independently and grounded against candidate patch features through patch-wise softmax assignment and importance-weighted aggregation, producing the atomic evidence score. Finally, query-wise z-score normalization calibrates both evidence scores, and weighted linear fusion produces the final retrieval score and ranking. We first formulate the ZS-CIR task in Sec. 3.1 . As illustrated in Fig. 2 , ASAP-CIR proceeds through three computational stages: target-state semantic reconstruction, multi-level target-state matching, and target-state evidence aggregation. For methodological organization, matching and evidence aggregation are presented together in Sec. 3.3 because both operate on the reconstructed representation without introducing additional trainable components. The first module, Target-State Semantic Reconstruction , uses an off-the-shelf MLLM to infer the completed visual state and express it at holistic and atomic levels. Holistic descriptions summarize the expected appearance and scene, whereas atomic semantics preserve fine-grained objects, attributes, relations, and other observable requirements. This stage moves transformation reasoning outside the CLIP text encoder and is described in Sec. 3.2 . The second module, Multi-Level Target-State Matching , evaluates each candidate using complementary evidence. Holistic state alignment measures overall image–text consistency, while atomic constraint grounding measures how strongly candidate patches support individual target-state facts. Their normalized scores are then aggregated to produce the final ranking. We present this process in Sec. 3.3 .

sections.heading: 3.1 Problem Definition
sections.text: We consider the training-free ZS-CIR setting, in which no annotated triplets of reference images, modification texts, and target images are used for optimization. All pretrained model parameters remain frozen, and retrieval is performed without task-specific training. Given a reference image I r I_{r} and a modification text T m T_{m} , the goal of composed image retrieval (CIR) is to rank images from a candidate gallery 𝒢 \mathcal{G} according to their consistency with the intended target semantics. The reference image provides the original visual content, while the modification text specifies the desired semantic changes relative to the reference image. Together, they form a composed query q = ( I r , T m ) q=(I_{r},T_{m}) . Given a candidate gallery 𝒢 = { I 1 , I 2 , … , I N } \mathcal{G}=\{I_{1},I_{2},\ldots,I_{N}\} , CIR aims to assign higher matching scores to valid target images than to irrelevant candidates. This formulation covers both single-target benchmarks such as FashionIQ and CIRR and multi-target benchmarks such as CIRCO. With S ⁡ ( ⋅ , ⋅ ) S(\cdot,\cdot) denoting the matching function between the composed query and a candidate image, retrieval can be viewed as ranking all candidates according to S ⁡ ( q , I i ) S(q,I_{i}) and returning the top-ranked images. A desirable retrieval model should therefore assign high scores to candidate images that both preserve the query-relevant visual content of the reference image and satisfy the semantic changes specified by the modification text.

sections.heading: 3.2 Target-State Semantic Reconstruction
sections.text: Given a composed query q = ( I r , T m ) q=(I_{r},T_{m}) , where I r I_{r} denotes the reference image and T m T_{m} denotes the modification text, the first module uses a frozen MLLM to jointly interpret both inputs and reconstruct the visual content expected in the target image. It expresses this inferred state through complementary holistic descriptions and atomic semantics without updating any model parameters. Formally, the reconstruction process is written as ( 𝒟 q , 𝒜 q ) = Φ MLLM ​ ( I r , T m , 𝒫 d ) , (\mathcal{D}_{q},\mathcal{A}_{q})=\Phi_{\mathrm{MLLM}}\left(I_{r},T_{m};\mathcal{P}_{d}\right), (1) where Φ MLLM \Phi_{\mathrm{MLLM}} denotes the frozen MLLM and 𝒫 d \mathcal{P}_{d} denotes the dataset-specific prompt used to express the inferred target state in a visually observable form. The output contains a holistic description set 𝒟 q \mathcal{D}_{q} and an importance-weighted atomic semantic set 𝒜 q \mathcal{A}_{q} . The former captures the overall appearance and scene-level state, while the latter decomposes that state into fine-grained visual requirements.

sections.heading: 3.2.1 Static Semantic Canonicalization
sections.text: The prompt 𝒫 d \mathcal{P}_{d} is designed to enforce two constraints. First, the generated text should describe the final target image directly, rather than explaining the editing process from the reference image. Second, each atomic semantic should correspond to a visually observable static fact, such as an object, attribute, relation, material, count, style, or scene cue. In other words, expressions such as “remove the dog” or “change the bottle to orange” are discouraged, while static formulations such as “a single dog is visible” or “an orange soft drink bottle is present” are preferred. This explicit constraint is important because it aligns the generated text with the static image-caption form on which CLIP-like models are pretrained. We use dataset-specific prompts because the preservation assumptions are different across benchmarks. In FashionIQ, the reference garment usually provides important identity and style information, so unchanged garment attributes should be retained unless they conflict with the modification. In CIRR and CIRCO, the modification may explicitly add, remove, or replace objects and scene context, so the MLLM is asked to infer which reference details should remain visible and which should be suppressed. This prompt design allows the parser to produce target semantics that are both static and adapted to each query.

sections.heading: 3.2.2 Holistic Target-State Representation
sections.text: To obtain a robust holistic representation of the target image, the MLLM generates K K semantically consistent yet linguistically diverse holistic descriptions: 𝒟 q = { d q k } k = 1 K , \mathcal{D}_{q}=\left\{d_{q}^{k}\right\}_{k=1}^{K}, (2) where d q k d_{q}^{k} denotes the k k -th holistic description and K K is the number of generated descriptions. Each d q k d_{q}^{k} is formulated as a standalone static image caption that directly describes the expected target image, rather than as an editing instruction describing how the reference image should be modified. In practice, we prompt the model to generate caption-style expressions, such as sentences beginning with “A photo of” or “A product photo of”. These descriptions characterize the target image from a global perspective, including its primary objects, attributes, scene context, and overall visual appearance. Generating multiple holistic descriptions provides complementary linguistic views of the same target semantics. Although these descriptions are semantically consistent, different expressions may emphasize different aspects of the target image. This reduces the risk that a single generated caption omits important discriminative information and provides a more comprehensive holistic representation for subsequent retrieval. More importantly, all generated descriptions remain in the form of static image captions, making them naturally compatible with the image–text matching paradigm of CLIP.

sections.heading: 3.2.3 Atomic Target-State Representation
sections.text: Although the holistic descriptions provide an overall representation of the expected target image, they may still fail to explicitly preserve all fine-grained requirements contained in the composed query. This limitation becomes more evident when the modification text involves multiple objects, attributes, spatial relations, stylistic changes, or other local visual constraints. Therefore, in parallel with holistic description generation, we further require the MLLM to decompose the inferred target semantics into a variable-size set of importance-weighted atomic semantics: 𝒜 q = { ( a q i , α q i ) } i = 1 N q . \mathcal{A}_{q}=\{(a_{q}^{i},\alpha_{q}^{i})\}_{i=1}^{N_{q}}. (3) where a q i a_{q}^{i} denotes the i i -th atomic semantic, α q i ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \alpha_{q}^{i}\in[0,1] denotes its corresponding importance weight, and N q N_{q} is the number of atomic semantics generated for query q q . Each atomic semantic is expressed as an independent static visual description that captures a specific fine-grained requirement of the desired target image. These requirements may correspond to objects, attributes, spatial relations, styles, counts, materials, scenes, or other visually observable constraints implied by the composed query. The importance weight α q i \alpha_{q}^{i} is a heuristic score estimated by the MLLM that indicates the relative retrieval relevance of the i i -th semantic requirement. Semantics that are directly related to the requested modification or are highly discriminative for the target are assigned larger weights, whereas less informative contextual details receive smaller weights. We do not treat these values as calibrated probabilities; instead, they provide a lightweight query prior for emphasizing more important visual requirements during atomic constraint grounding. Since N q N_{q} is query-dependent, the proposed representation naturally adapts to different levels of semantic complexity. A simple query may require only a small number of atomic semantics, whereas a more complex modification text can be decomposed into a larger set of static visual requirements. This variable-size representation avoids forcing heterogeneous queries into a fixed semantic structure and allows ASAP-CIR to preserve query-specific information more faithfully. The importance-weighted atomic semantic set 𝒜 q \mathcal{A}_{q} is directly used in the subsequent atomic constraint grounding stage. Unlike the holistic descriptions in 𝒟 q \mathcal{D}_{q} , which characterize the expected target image from an overall perspective, 𝒜 q \mathcal{A}_{q} focuses on explicit fine-grained constraints that should be satisfied by the retrieved image. The term “atomic” indicates that each unit describes a compact static visual fact. The two representations therefore provide complementary views of the target semantics: 𝒟 q \mathcal{D}_{q} captures holistic semantic consistency, while 𝒜 q \mathcal{A}_{q} preserves fine-grained atomic requirements. Overall, the proposed parsing module transforms the original composed query into two complementary static target representations: the holistic description set 𝒟 q \mathcal{D}_{q} , which summarizes the overall semantics of the expected target image, and the importance-weighted atomic semantic set 𝒜 q \mathcal{A}_{q} , which explicitly represents its fine-grained visual constraints. These two representations are subsequently used for holistic state alignment and atomic constraint grounding, respectively. The MLLM operates only on the query side; candidate images are represented directly by CLIP. Their features can therefore be precomputed offline, avoiding gallery-side MLLM inference while preserving training-free retrieval efficiency.

We use a frozen vision-language model with an image encoder E v E_{v} and a text encoder E t E_{t} to compute candidate-level holistic similarities and atomic-to-patch similarities, from which complementary holistic and atomic evidence scores are derived.

sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Datasets. Following recent ZS-CIR studies ( Lim et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) , we evaluate ASAP-CIR on three widely used composed image retrieval benchmarks: FashionIQ ( Wu et al., 2021 ) , CIRR ( Liu et al., 2021 ) , and CIRCO ( Baldrati et al., 2023 ) . FashionIQ is a fashion-domain retrieval benchmark containing three categories, namely Dress, Shirt, and Toptee. We evaluate on the validation split and report recall at rank k k (R@ k k ), with k ∈ { 10 , 50 } k\in\{10,50\} , for each category, together with their average over the three categories. CIRR is an open-domain benchmark constructed from real-life images sourced from NLVR2. It augments reference–target image pairs with human-written relative captions that describe the intended semantic change, thereby emphasizing fine-grained discrimination among visually similar natural images. CIRR provides both full-gallery and visually restricted subset evaluation protocols. We evaluate on the test1 split and report full-gallery R@ k k with k ∈ { 1 , 5 , 10 , 50 } k\in\{1,5,10,50\} ; to keep the main comparison focused on this setting, we do not report subset recall. CIRCO is built from the COCO 2017 unlabeled image set and provides multiple ground-truth target images for each query. It contains 123,403 candidate images and 800 test queries. Following the official evaluation protocol, we report mean average precision at rank k k (mAP@ k k ), with k ∈ { 5 , 10 , 25 , 50 } k\in\{5,10,25,50\} . Baselines. We compare ASAP-CIR with representative zero-shot composed image retrieval methods using reported backbone architecture groups whenever available. The compared methods include training-based or language-supervised approaches, such as Pic2Word ( Saito et al., 2023 ) , SEARLE ( Baldrati et al., 2023 ) , LinCIR ( Gu et al., 2024 ) , FlowCIR ( He et al., 2026 ) , DiffComp ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , and TT-RLDR ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) . We also compare with recent training-free methods that rely on foundation models or test-time reasoning, including CIReVL ( Karthik et al., 2024 ) , LDRE ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , AutoCIR ( Cheng et al., 2025 ) , OSrCIR ( Tang et al., 2025 ) , and STiTch ( Li et al., 2026 ) . In the tables, T-Free denotes whether a method is training-free. We group methods by their reported visual encoder architecture for readability, while noting that exact pretrained checkpoints, preprocessing pipelines, and implementation details may differ across papers. Following common practice, the best and second-best results within each backbone group are shown in bold and underlined , respectively. Implementation Details. ASAP-CIR is a training-free method and does not use any CIR triplets for optimization. We use Qwen3.6-27B as the frozen MLLM for static semantic parsing of queries. In our implementation, the number of holistic descriptions is controlled by the hyperparameter num-target-descriptions , and we set K = 3 K=3 by default. If fewer than K K valid descriptions are produced, the last valid description is repeated until the number reaches K K ; if more than K K descriptions are produced, only the first K K descriptions are retained. The prompt requests 4–7 semantic lines, but generation is not constrained to an exact count. All valid atomic lines are retained without forced truncation, so the resulting N q N_{q} remains query dependent. Candidate images are not processed by the MLLM; instead, their visual features are extracted and cached before retrieval. For CLIP-based matching, we use OpenCLIP backbones, including ViT-B/32, ViT-L/14, and ViT-G/14, with LAION pretrained weights. Unless otherwise specified, ViT-L/14 with laion2b_s32b_b82k is used as the default backbone. We apply TargetPad preprocessing with a targetpad-ratio of 1.25 and perform feature extraction in float16 precision. During MLLM inference, all generated results are saved as structured query semantic files and reused for retrieval. This avoids repeated MLLM calls when testing different fusion weights, temperatures, or CLIP backbones. For holistic state alignment, the three generated holistic descriptions are encoded independently and then averaged after feature normalization. For atomic constraint grounding, each atomic semantic is encoded as a short static text query and matched against patch features extracted from the candidate image encoder. All candidate image features are cached under the project directory, so changing retrieval hyperparameters does not require re-encoding the image gallery. Hardware and retrieval settings. MLLM parsing is performed on six NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPUs, while retrieval and feature scoring are performed on a single RTX 3090 GPU. Candidate image features are cached in advance, so retrieval only requires text encoding, candidate-feature loading, and matrix-based similarity computation. We use an atomic grounding temperature of 0.07. The holistic and atomic evidence scores undergo query-wise z-score normalization before fusion. Unless otherwise stated, the holistic/atomic fusion weights ( λ g , λ l ) (\lambda_{g},\lambda_{l}) are set to 0.90/0.10 for FashionIQ, 0.85/0.15 for CIRR, and 0.95/0.05 for CIRCO. These dataset-specific weights are selected from coarse preliminary sweeps and then fixed for the reported runs; the CIRCO sensitivity analysis in Sec. 4.4 makes this choice transparent.

sections.heading: 4.2 Benchmark Performance
sections.text: We compare ASAP-CIR with representative ZS-CIR methods on FashionIQ, CIRR, and CIRCO. The results are reported in Table 1 , Table 2 , and Table 3 , respectively. Overall, ASAP-CIR achieves competitive performance across the three benchmarks and shows its clearest advantage on CIRCO, where multiple ground-truth targets require a retrieval model to capture diverse yet accurate target semantics.

sections.heading: 4.2.1 FashionIQ
sections.text: Table 1 presents the results on FashionIQ. With ViT-B/32, ASAP-CIR obtains 30.99 average R@10 and 53.20 average R@50; with ViT-L/14, it reaches 35.00 and 55.02, respectively. Within the reported comparison set, the method performs particularly well on Dress and Toptee under ViT-L/14, suggesting that the parsed atomic semantics can capture discriminative attributes such as color, texture, sleeve length, silhouette, and style. Its lower Shirt scores indicate that static semantic parsing does not uniformly resolve all fine-grained fashion retrieval cases, particularly when visually similar garments differ in subtle structural details. It is worth noting that FashionIQ descriptions are usually short and attribute-centric. A single holistic description may already capture the dominant garment category, but it may underrepresent subtle style changes that determine the correct target among visually similar products. Atomic evidence complements holistic evidence by assigning explicit weights to these fine-grained attributes. Therefore, even without any training on FashionIQ triplets, ASAP-CIR can remain competitive with methods that rely on learned textual inversion or task-specific composition.

sections.heading: 4.2.2 CIRR
sections.text: Table 2 reports the results on CIRR. ASAP-CIR obtains 28.41 R@1 with ViT-B/32 and 32.80 R@1 with ViT-L/14. The latter exceeds AutoCIR by 0.99 points under the same backbone grouping. However, ASAP-CIR becomes less competitive at larger retrieval depths, where DiffComp and AutoCIR obtain stronger results. This behavior may reflect the emphasis of our scoring function on precise semantic satisfaction rather than explicit candidate-pool expansion. CIRR therefore remains a challenging setting for the current formulation, particularly when diverse candidates share similar global content. This behavior may be related to the design of our method. Since ASAP-CIR converts the query into explicit target semantic requirements, candidates that violate key atomic constraints tend to be penalized during atomic constraint grounding. Such scoring can help select a highly precise top-ranked image, but may reduce the diversity of lower-ranked candidates. We consider this a reasonable trade-off for CIRR, where the top-1 result is particularly important for evaluating whether the composed query is correctly grounded.

sections.heading: 4.2.3 CIRCO
sections.text: As shown in Table 3 , ASAP-CIR obtains strong results on CIRCO under both ViT-L/14 and ViT-G/14 backbones. With ViT-L/14, it reaches 35.49, 36.46, 39.21, and 40.35 mAP at k = { 5 , 10 , 25 , 50 } k=\{5,10,25,50\} , improving over STiTch by 9.94, 10.19, 10.40, and 10.36 points, respectively. The improvement is consistent across all retrieval depths. With the stronger ViT-G/14 backbone, ASAP-CIR reaches 37.06, 38.47, 41.44, and 42.52 mAP, exceeding STiTch by 2.66, 2.91, 3.37, and 2.50 points. These results indicate that converting dynamic modification requirements into explicit holistic descriptions and atomic semantics provides an effective retrieval signal for CIRCO, where the target images may satisfy the query in multiple plausible ways. The consistent advantage on CIRCO is aligned with our motivation. Unlike single-target evaluation, mAP rewards methods that can rank multiple semantically valid images ahead of distractors. The holistic descriptions generated by the MLLM provide broad target coverage, while the importance-weighted atomic semantics help suppress candidates that match only the reference image or only a subset of the required changes. This combination is particularly beneficial for queries involving multiple acceptable targets, since the retrieval model must capture the common static semantics shared by all valid answers rather than overfitting to one textual expression. sections.heading: 4.3 Target-State Alignment Analysis in Pretrained VLMs
sections.text: Beyond benchmark comparisons, we test the central representation hypothesis directly: does a description of the completed target state align with target candidates more reliably than a transformation-oriented composed query? This diagnostic does not claim a universal inability of CLIP to understand dynamic language. Instead, it isolates a controlled textual setting relevant to CIR and measures the representation mismatch between transition instructions and completed visual states. We construct a synthetic text-only evaluation set with Qwen3-32B.

sections.heading: 4.3.1 Controlled Text-Only Evaluation
sections.text: Specifically, we ask Qwen3-32B to synthesize 4,096 structured six-tuples. Each tuple consists of an operation type, a static reference description, a dynamic modification instruction, a static target description, a paraphrased target-side static query, and a set of hard negative descriptions. The operation types cover eight representative dynamic semantic categories: addition, removal, replacement, attribute change, relation change, count change, style change, and background change. Each category contains 512 samples. For each sample, we compare two CLIP-based retrieval settings, hereafter termed the target-side static query formulation and the dynamic composed query formulation. In the static setting, the query is expressed as a static target description. In the dynamic setting, the exact template used by the implementation is “ REFERENCE, but INSTRUCTION ”, where REFERENCE and INSTRUCTION are replaced by the static reference description and the lowercased dynamic instruction, respectively. Both queries are encoded by the same CLIP text encoder and used to retrieve the corresponding target from the target and hard-negative candidates. Therefore, the only difference between the two settings is whether the query is represented as static semantics of the target or dynamic modification semantics. For conciseness, we refer to these settings below as the static and dynamic formulations, respectively. For implementation, we evaluate three OpenCLIP text encoders, including ViT-B/32, ViT-L/14, and ViT-G/14, with LAION pretrained weights. All reference descriptions, dynamic queries, static queries describing the target, target descriptions, and hard negatives are encoded by the corresponding CLIP text encoder and ℓ 2 \ell_{2} normalized before similarity computation. For each synthesized sample, the retrieval gallery consists of the ground-truth target description and its hard negatives. We report R@1 by checking whether the query retrieves the corresponding target description as the nearest neighbor under cosine similarity. This design isolates the semantic behavior of the text encoder of CLIP and removes the influence of image encoding or dataset-specific visual noise. The synthetic evaluation set contains 4,096 Qwen3-32B generated samples across eight dynamic semantic categories. Table 4 summarizes the overall results across the three backbones. The static query formulation consistently achieves much higher R@1 than the dynamic formulation. With ViT-B/32, static queries obtain 81.52% R@1, while dynamic queries only obtain 29.69%. With the default ViT-L/14 backbone, the gap increases to 54.22 points, with 83.23% R@1 for static queries and 29.00% R@1 for dynamic queries. The same phenomenon remains under the stronger ViT-G/14 backbone, where static queries reach 86.21% R@1 but dynamic queries still remain at 32.59%. These results suggest that simply scaling the CLIP backbone improves static semantic matching, but does not eliminate the gap between static and dynamic query formulations under this controlled protocol.

sections.heading: 4.3.2 Operation-Wise Analysis
sections.text: Fig. 3 further shows the results for individual operations under the default ViT-L/14 text encoder. The degradation is particularly severe for removal, replacement, and count change, where the dynamic formulation obtains much lower R@1 than the static formulation. For example, dynamic queries obtain 0.00% R@1 on removal, 3.32% on replacement, and 4.88% on count change. Similar trends are also observed with ViT-B/32 and ViT-G/14. Addition is a notable exception: under ViT-L/14 and ViT-G/14, the dynamic formulation reaches 93.16% and 95.51% R@1, slightly exceeding the corresponding static results of 90.82% and 93.95%. This behavior is plausible because an added object can often be matched as an ordinary visible noun phrase without resolving negation or replacing a source-state concept. We provide the complete visualizations for individual operations and feature distributions for ViT-B/32 and ViT-G/14 in the appendix. Overall, the results indicate that, in this synthetic text-only setting, directly encoding instructions combining the reference and modification is less reliable for operations that require suppressing or transforming source-state semantics, while simple addition can remain well aligned with CLIP’s text space. sections.heading: 4.3.3 Feature-Space Analysis
sections.text: To further inspect the feature distribution, we randomly sample 50 queries from each of the eight operation types and visualize their default ViT-L/14 text features, as shown in Fig. 4 . The static query features are generally closer to the corresponding target features, while the dynamic query features are more frequently displaced away from the target semantics. Combined with the consistent R@1 gaps across ViT-B/32, ViT-L/14, and ViT-G/14, this observation provides feature-level evidence that target-state formulations are better aligned with target descriptions than transformation-oriented formulations in our diagnostic setting. This supports the central design choice of ASAP-CIR: reconstruct the state to be retrieved before entering the pretrained vision-language space.

CIRCO is selected because its multiple ground-truth targets provide a fine-grained test of whether candidates preserve the intended target state rather than merely one textual realization. We examine the complementary roles of holistic and atomic evidence, importance weighting of atomic semantics, robustness to the choice of MLLM parser, and the calibration and aggregation of atomic evidence. sections.heading: 4.4.3 Temperature of Atomic Evidence Grounding
sections.text: The atomic constraint grounding module computes the soft semantic coverage score of each atomic semantic by applying a softmax operation over candidate patch features. The temperature τ \tau controls the sharpness of this atomic-to-patch assignment. As shown in Fig. 5 (a), ASAP-CIR is relatively insensitive to the temperature within a reasonable range. When τ \tau varies from 0.03 to 0.15, all four mAP metrics remain stable, suggesting that atomic constraint grounding does not rely on a carefully tuned temperature. The best or near-best results are obtained around τ = 0.07 \tau=0.07 and τ = 0.10 \tau=0.10 . In our main experiments, we set τ = 0.07 \tau=0.07 because it provides consistently strong performance across different retrieval depths while keeping the atomic-to-patch assignment sufficiently selective.

sections.heading: 4.4.4 Target-State Evidence Aggregation
sections.text: We then evaluate the contribution of holistic and atomic evidence by varying the holistic weight λ g \lambda_{g} from 0.75 to 1.00, with the atomic weight set to λ l = 1 − λ g \lambda_{l}=1-\lambda_{g} . As shown in Fig. 5 (b), holistic evidence alone already achieves competitive performance, suggesting that the holistic descriptions generated by the MLLM provide a strong static representation of the composed query. However, introducing a small amount of atomic evidence consistently improves ranking quality. In particular, the setting λ g = 0.95 \lambda_{g}=0.95 and λ l = 0.05 \lambda_{l}=0.05 achieves the best performance on mAP@10, mAP@25, and mAP@50, while λ g = 0.90 \lambda_{g}=0.90 and λ l = 0.10 \lambda_{l}=0.10 gives the best mAP@5. This suggests that importance-weighted atomic semantics complement holistic descriptions by emphasizing fine-grained requirements that may be weakened in a single overall caption. Meanwhile, assigning an overly large atomic weight degrades performance, since atomic semantics alone cannot fully represent the overall target appearance. Therefore, we use λ g = 0.95 \lambda_{g}=0.95 and λ l = 0.05 \lambda_{l}=0.05 as the default fusion weights for CIRCO.

sections.heading: 4.5.1 Successful Target-State Reconstruction
sections.text: The first successful case requires the hyena to be running away. The reconstructed holistic state preserves the animal and scene context, while the atomic action constraint distinguishes the target motion from visually similar animal images. In the second case, the query introduces a wooden log into the reference scene. Holistic alignment maintains the overall scene content, whereas atomic grounding emphasizes the newly added object and suppresses candidates that preserve only the reference appearance. The third case changes the water to blue. Here, the holistic description retains the surrounding scene, while the explicit color constraint helps separate the target from candidates with similar content but a different water appearance. These cases illustrate the complementary roles of holistic state alignment and atomic constraint grounding under different modification types.

sections.heading: 4.5.2 Failure Cases and Remaining Boundaries
sections.text: The failure cases expose the distinction between reconstructing a target state and grounding it precisely. In the example “put the human in background”, the parser can express the desired entities, yet the retriever fails to resolve their spatial relation. In the example “change to real soft drink bottle in orange”, the top-ranked candidates contain relevant soft drink bottles but do not match the expected orange instance. ASAP-CIR may therefore remain unreliable for precise relations, subtle attributes, or instance-level distinctions among visually similar candidates. Target-state reconstruction improves the query representation, but it does not by itself solve every visual-grounding ambiguity.

sections.heading: 5 Discussion
sections.text: The results support a representation-centered interpretation of ZS-CIR. A composed query naturally describes a transition, whereas a retrieval candidate depicts a completed state. ASAP-CIR reduces this asymmetry by reconstructing the expected state before matching, allowing the pretrained vision-language model to operate closer to its image–caption alignment regime. The resulting representation is deliberately multi-level: holistic descriptions retain overall coherence, while atomic semantics preserve requirements that can be diluted in a single caption. The diagnostic results also clarify when this principle is most useful. The largest static–dynamic gaps occur for removal, replacement, and count change, where successful retrieval requires suppressing or transforming source-state concepts. Addition is less dependent on reconstruction because the added concept can often be matched as an ordinary visible noun phrase. Thus, the benefit is operation dependent rather than universal, and the controlled analysis should be interpreted as evidence for the formulation under the studied protocol rather than as a general claim about every CLIP capability. Finally, semantic reconstruction and visual grounding remain distinct problems. An MLLM may correctly describe the target state while CLIP patch features still fail to localize a subtle relation, distinguish a specific instance, or resolve visually ambiguous attributes. Parser errors can likewise propagate into retrieval. Future work can therefore build on target-state reconstruction while improving uncertainty modeling, relation-aware grounding, and parser–retriever interaction without requiring supervised CIR triplets.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we studied how composed retrieval intent should be represented for pretrained vision-language retrieval. Our controlled analysis shows that, under the considered text-only protocol, target-state descriptions are more reliably aligned with intended targets than formulations that combine a reference description and modification instruction. We proposed ASAP-CIR, a training-free realization of target-state reconstruction that combines holistic descriptions with importance-weighted atomic semantics, followed by holistic state alignment, atomic constraint grounding, and calibrated target-state evidence aggregation. Experiments on FashionIQ, CIRR, and CIRCO demonstrate the utility of this formulation, with its clearest gains on CIRCO. The results also expose important boundaries: performance remains sensitive to parser quality, complex spatial relations, subtle instance-level grounding, and dataset-specific retrieval structure. We hope this representation-centered view encourages future work to examine not only how multimodal signals are composed, but also how user intent should be formulated before it enters a pretrained vision-language retrieval space.

sections.heading: 7 Dataset-Specific MLLM Prompts
sections.text: This appendix provides the query MLLM prompts used by ASAP-CIR. The prompts are directly taken from the implementation. Following the prompt presentation style of recent training-free ZS-CIR works, we show each prompt as a boxed block with a short functional description. Each dataset shares the same compact output instruction and then uses a dataset-specific task prompt. Prompt A: Shared Output Format Instruction Function. This shared instruction standardizes all MLLM responses into holistic descriptions and importance-weighted atomic semantics. The prompt’s D-line “global caption” field corresponds to the holistic descriptions used in the paper. ⬇ Return compact retrieval content only . Every output sentence will be encoded by CLIP , so it must look like a natural web image caption . Use exactly this line format : D1 : one CLIP - style global caption D2 : one CLIP - style global caption D3 : one CLIP - style global caption S : scope | one atomic CLIP - style visual phrase or caption | importance Every S line must contain exactly two vertical bars and three fields : scope , phrase , importance . Never output an S line without an importance score . Allowed S scopes are exactly : global , atomic . Use global only for one complete caption summary ; use atomic for every local object , attribute , relation , scene , style , color , count , state , or material phrase . Importance is a number from 0.20 to 1.00. Use numeric importance with two decimals , for example 1.00, 0.85, 0.60, or 0.40. Do not output JSON , markdown , explanations , reasoning , bullet markers , or extra text . D lines should usually start with caption phrases such as ’ A photo of ’, ’ A close - up photo of ’, ’ A product photo of ’, or ’ An image of ’. S lines should be short caption noun phrases or simple visual captions , not analytical sentences . Avoid meta phrases such as ’ the target image shows ’, ’ the target image ’, ’ the image shows ’, ’ visible in the image ’, ’ main subject ’, ’ query ’, or ’ retrieval ’. Do not mention the reference image , source image , original image , modification text , or editing operation . Forbidden output words and phrases : target image , reference , original , source , modify , modified , edit , edited , add , added , remove , removed , replace , replaced , change , changed , become , instead , compared with , different from , same as , remain , remains , unchanged , no longer , without . If the modification implies absence , write only positive visible target facts , not negative facts . If the modification implies identity or size preservation , describe the visible target size / shape directly , not its relation to another image . Prefer fewer high - confidence S lines over many weak S lines . Prompt B: FashionIQ Static Semantic Parsing for Queries Function. This prompt focuses the MLLM on fashion-specific target attributes such as garment category, color, material, texture, pattern, fit, silhouette, and style. ⬇ Task : FashionIQ composed fashion retrieval . You receive a reference fashion image and a modification text . Infer the desired fashion item from both inputs . Use the image to identify visually salient garment details , but write only standalone CLIP - style captions . Focus on clothing category , color , material , texture , pattern , sleeve length , neckline , fit , silhouette , decorations , and style . Assign high importance to fashion details related to the modification , medium importance to preserved salient garment details , and low importance to unrelated pose / background . All D and S lines must be natural caption text . Do not write relative phrases such as " different from the reference " or " same as the reference ". Produce 3 D lines and 4 to 7 S lines . Example : Modification text : " is shiny and silver with shorter sleeves and fit and flare " D1 : A product photo of a shiny silver fit - and - flare { fashion_type } with short sleeves . D2 : A catalog photo of a short - sleeved silver { fashion_type } with a shiny finish and a fit - and - flare silhouette . D3 : A fashion product image of a shiny silver short - sleeved { fashion_type } with a flared shape . S : global | A shiny silver fit - and - flare { fashion_type } with short sleeves . | 1.00 S : atomic | A { fashion_type }. | 0.80 S : atomic | Shiny silver fabric . | 1.00 S : atomic | Short sleeves . | 0.95 S : atomic | A fit - and - flare silhouette . | 0.95 S : atomic | A polished fashion product photo . | 0.60 Fashion type : { fashion_type } Modification text : "{ modification_text }" Prompt C: CIRR Static Semantic Parsing for Queries Function. This prompt converts general composed-image modifications into standalone static visual facts of the target, including objects, counts, attributes, relations, scenes, and backgrounds. ⬇ Task : CIRR composed image retrieval . You receive a reference image and a modification text . Infer the desired final visual content from both inputs . Convert dynamic modifications into static visible caption facts . Focus on objects , people , animals , object count , attributes , pose , object condition , spatial relations , interactions , scene , background , and composition . For removals or negative instructions , describe only the visible content that should be present . Preserve unchanged content only when it is visually important or likely useful for retrieval . All D and S lines must be natural CLIP - style captions . Do not describe editing operations or compare with the reference image . Produce 3 D lines and 4 to 7 S lines . Example : Modification text : " remove all but one dog and add a woman hugging it " D1 : A photo of a woman hugging one dog . D2 : A natural image of one dog being hugged by a woman . sections.heading: 8 Backbone Analysis
sections.text: This appendix provides additional results across backbones for the controlled dynamic semantic analysis in Sec. 4.3 . In the main paper, we use ViT-L/14 as the representative backbone for detailed operation-wise and feature-level visualization. Here, we further report the corresponding results for ViT-B/32 and ViT-G/14. The evaluation protocol is exactly the same as in Sec. 4.3 : for each synthesized six-tuple, the target-side static query and the dynamic composed query are encoded by the same CLIP text encoder and retrieve the target description from the gallery containing the target and hard negatives. (a) ViT-B/32 (b) ViT-G/14 Figure 7: Operation-wise R@1 comparison between target-side static and dynamic composed query formulations under additional OpenCLIP backbones. As shown in Fig. 7 , the operation-wise behavior is consistent with the ViT-L/14 results in the main paper. Under ViT-B/32, static queries obtain 81.52% overall R@1, while dynamic queries obtain only 29.69%. Under the stronger ViT-G/14, static queries improve to 86.21%, but dynamic queries still remain at 32.59%. In both cases, removal, replacement, and count change remain particularly difficult for dynamic query encoding. For example, ViT-B/32 obtains only 0.20%, 3.32%, and 4.69% dynamic R@1 on removal, replacement, and count change, respectively; ViT-G/14 obtains 0.00%, 2.73%, and 13.67% on the same categories. These results further suggest that the observed behavior is not specific to a single CLIP backbone. (a) ViT-B/32 (b) ViT-G/14 Figure 8: Target-anchored PCA projections under additional OpenCLIP backbones. For each operation type, 50 samples are randomly selected. Target-side static query features are generally closer to the target features than dynamic composed query features. Fig. 8 further visualizes the target-anchored feature distributions for ViT-B/32 and ViT-G/14. Although the projected layouts vary across encoders, the qualitative pattern remains stable: static queries describing the target tend to be closer to the corresponding target descriptions, whereas dynamic composed queries are more frequently displaced away from the target semantics. Together with the quantitative results in Table 4 , these supplementary results indicate that the observed gap between static and dynamic formulations is persistent across backbone scales. This provides additional evidence for the core motivation of ASAP-CIR: dynamic modification instructions can benefit from being converted into static semantics of the target before CLIP-based matching.

This task exhibits an unusual representational asymmetry: the modification text specifies a transition from the reference state, whereas retrieval candidates depict completed target states. This creates a representation mismatch for zero-shot methods that query pretrained vision-language spaces directly with transformation-oriented language. We study this mismatch and reformulate zero-shot composed image retrieval as target-state reconstruction followed by retrieval. We instantiate this formulation with ASAP-CIR , a training-free framework that reconstructs a static target representation using a frozen multimodal large language model (MLLM). The representation combines multiple holistic descriptions with a variable set of importance-weighted atomic semantics, thereby preserving both overall target identity and fine-grained visual constraints. Retrieval then integrates holistic state alignment, atomic constraint grounding, and calibrated target-state evidence aggregation. A controlled text-only diagnostic shows that target-side static query formulations achieve more reliable retrieval than dynamic composed query formulations, particularly when source-state semantics must be suppressed or transformed. Experiments on FashionIQ, CIRR, and CIRCO further characterize the effectiveness and limitations of this representation principle, with the clearest gains on the multi-target CIRCO benchmark. These results show that how composed intent is represented before retrieval is a consequential design choice, distinct from the choice of retrieval backbone itself. keywords Multimodal learning, composed image retrieval, pretrained vision-language models, zero-shot composed image retrieval 1 Introduction Composed image retrieval (CIR) enables users to search for a desired image through a visual reference and natural-language feedback. Unlike conventional text-to-image retrieval, however, CIR does not directly provide a description of the target. It provides evidence about a reference state together with an instruction that specifies how this state should change. The retrieval system must infer the completed target state before it can compare the query with candidate images. This capability supports interactive product search, fashion recommendation, visual editing assistance, and open-domain image search, but also makes CIR fundamentally different from ordinary image-text matching. Existing CIR methods can be roughly grouped into supervised and zero-shot paradigms. Supervised methods learn image-text composition from annotated triplets and can achieve strong performance when sufficient training data are available ( Vo et al., 2019 ; Baldrati et al., 2022 ; Han et al., 2023 ; Song et al., 2024 ) . Collecting such triplets is expensive, however, and models trained on fixed datasets may not generalize to new domains or unseen user intents. Zero-shot CIR (ZS-CIR) instead reuses pretrained vision-language models (VLMs), especially Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP), or employs large language models (LLMs) and multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to infer target-related text ( Saito et al., 2023 ; Baldrati et al., 2023 ; Karthik et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Tang et al., 2025 ) . Although this removes task-specific training, it exposes a more fundamental issue: the input semantics describe a transition, while the retrieval space is organized around observable visual states. We refer to this issue as the representation mismatch in ZS-CIR. A modification such as “remove the person”, “make the bottle orange”, or “add a wooden log” denotes an operation rather than a completed visual state. Directly encoding such language may preserve removed entities, superseded attributes, or editing predicates that should not be visible in the target. The difficulty is therefore not merely to compose an image and a sentence; it is to represent the intended target state in a pretrained image-text space that was not explicitly trained to execute state transitions. Our central insight is to reconstruct the target state before retrieval instead of asking a pretrained VLM to perform an implicit state transition inside its embedding space. Target-state reconstruction canonicalizes diverse dynamic instructions into static descriptions of what should be visible. Yet one caption is not sufficient for every composed query. The intended state has complementary holistic and atomic structure: holistic descriptions preserve target identity and scene coherence, whereas atomic semantics retain changed attributes, counts, relations, and newly introduced objects as explicit visual constraints. We therefore represent the reconstructed state as a static target representation containing both levels. MLLM reasoning remains restricted to the query side, while candidate features can be precomputed for efficient retrieval. Figure 1: Motivation of ASAP-CIR. To examine whether this reformulation is supported by the behavior of pretrained vision-language representations, we further conduct a controlled text-only diagnostic study. Under this protocol, static target descriptions retrieve the intended target descriptions more reliably than formulations that combine a reference description and modification instruction. This result does not imply a universal inability of CLIP to encode dynamic language; instead, it shows that query formulation materially affects retrieval alignment in the considered CIR setting. Benchmark experiments further reveal that the benefit is dataset dependent: it is most pronounced on CIRCO, while FashionIQ and CIRR expose limitations in fine-grained garment discrimination and deeper candidate ranking. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: • We identify and formulate a representation mismatch in ZS-CIR: transformation-oriented instructions are used to query pretrained image-text spaces whose candidates express completed visual states. We consequently reformulate ZS-CIR as target-state reconstruction followed by retrieval. • We introduce a multi-level static target representation that jointly preserves holistic semantics and fine-grained atomic constraints. ASAP-CIR provides a training-free realization of this principle and a structured interface between frozen MLLM reasoning and pretrained VLM retrieval. • We establish controlled evidence that target-state formulations are better aligned with pretrained CLIP representations for several transformation types, and evaluate the resulting retrieval behavior on FashionIQ, CIRR, and CIRCO, including its benefits and remaining boundaries. 2 Related Work 2.1 Composed Image Retrieval Composed image retrieval retrieves images according to a reference image and a natural-language modification. Unlike conventional image retrieval, in which a query is expressed through a single modality, CIR requires the retrieval model to preserve query-relevant visual content from the reference while satisfying the changes expressed in language. Existing CIR methods can be broadly divided into supervised and zero-shot paradigms. Supervised methods learn this composition from annotated triplets of reference images, modification texts, and target images. Early approaches such as TIRG ( Vo et al., 2019 ) learn dedicated feature composition modules to combine visual and textual cues, while later methods further exploit pretrained vision-language models, cross-modal attention, or task-specific pretraining objectives to improve composed retrieval performance ( Baldrati et al., 2022 ; Han et al., 2023 ; Song et al., 2024 ; Fu et al., 2026 ) . Although these methods achieve strong performance when training triplets are available, their reliance on annotated CIR data limits their scalability to new domains and retrieval scenarios. In addition, supervised models tend to inherit the semantic distribution of the training triplets, making it difficult to handle rare or open-ended modification intents without collecting new annotations. Several benchmarks have been proposed to support CIR research. Fashion200k ( Han et al., 2017 ) is an early fashion-domain benchmark that connects product images with relative textual feedback. FashionIQ ( Wu et al., 2021 ) further provides human-written natural language feedback for fashion retrieval across multiple garment categories. CIRR ( Liu et al., 2021 ) extends composed retrieval to real-life open-domain images and introduces both full-gallery and subset evaluation protocols, while CIRCO ( Baldrati et al., 2023 ) builds a challenging COCO-based benchmark with multiple valid target images for each query. To reduce the dependence on CIR triplets, recent studies have increasingly focused on ZS-CIR. One representative line of work follows the textual inversion paradigm. Pic2Word ( Saito et al., 2023 ) maps an input image into a pseudo-word token in the CLIP text embedding space, enabling the composed query to be represented as a text prompt. SEARLE ( Baldrati et al., 2023 ) improves this idea through a textual inversion mechanism that represents the reference image as a pseudo-word token and composes it with the relative caption. Subsequent methods such as LinCIR ( Gu et al., 2024 ) reduce the need for image-text supervision by using language-only training, while DeG ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , MOA ( Li et al., 2025 ) , and CoCo-IR ( Cao et al., 2026 ) further study data-efficient generalization, object-aware pseudo-word learning, and contextual composed retrieval. Beyond textual inversion, recent ZS-CIR methods also explore difference-aware composition, semantic flow, geodesic semantic expansion, and reward-guided test-time optimization, as represented by DiffComp, FlowCIR, G-MIXER, and TT-RLDR ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ; Lim et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) . These methods are elegant and efficient because they reuse or adapt the pretrained CLIP image-text alignment space. In textual inversion methods, however, the pseudo-word representation of the reference image is typically inserted into a prompt together with the original modification text. Consequently, explicit transition expressions such as removal, replacement, or attribute change may remain in the composed prompt and be passed directly to the CLIP text encoder. Such methods therefore implicitly assume that CLIP can interpret these dynamic modification semantics and combine them correctly with the pseudo-word representation. Another recent line of work explores training-free ZS-CIR with LLMs or MLLMs. CIReVL ( Karthik et al., 2024 ) first captions the reference image with a VLM and then uses an LLM to rewrite the composed query into target descriptions for CLIP retrieval. LDRE ( Yang et al., 2024 ) further generates dense reference captions and performs LLM-based divergent reasoning, followed by semantic-relevance-weighted caption ensemble. PrediCIR ( Tang et al., 2025 ) predicts missing target-relevant information with a world model, and CoTMR ( Sun et al., 2025 ) introduces chain-of-thought multi-scale reasoning for training-free retrieval. AutoCIR ( Cheng et al., 2025 ) formulates ZS-CIR as automatic multi-agent collaboration with planning, retrieval, and correction agents, while OSrCIR ( Tang et al., 2025 ) employs one-stage reflective chain-of-thought reasoning with an MLLM before retrieval. More recent methods such as STiTch ( Li et al., 2026 ) and WISER ( Wang et al., 2026 ) further improve training-free retrieval through semantic transition and transportation, wider search, deeper reasoning, or adaptive fusion. These approaches demonstrate that external reasoning can reduce reliance on directly encoding raw modification text. Because some of them infer descriptions of the target, their outputs may incidentally avoid explicit transition words and contain implicit static target semantics. However, static semantic formulation is generally a by-product rather than an explicit constraint: generated descriptions are not necessarily required to exclude source-state or transition-oriented expressions, nor are target requirements systematically organized at complementary semantic levels. Their primary emphasis is instead on composition, reasoning, search, or fusion. Accordingly, the distinction of ASAP-CIR is not merely the use of an MLLM or an additional patch-level matching branch. Existing methods mainly investigate how reference and modification information should be composed, reasoned over, or refined; our work instead asks how the inferred target state should be represented before retrieval. ASAP-CIR answers this question through a multi-level static target representation that combines holistic descriptions with importance-weighted atomic semantics, thereby making query representation itself an explicit component of retrieval design. 2.2 Vision-Language Models for CIR Vision-language models (VLMs) have become a fundamental component of modern multimodal learning, as they provide a shared representation space for visual and textual information. Among them, CLIP, introduced by Radford et al. ( Radford et al., 2021 ) , is one of the most representative models for open-vocabulary visual understanding. CLIP is trained on large-scale image-text pairs using a contrastive learning objective, where matched image-text pairs are pulled closer and mismatched pairs are pushed apart in a shared embedding space. This simple yet scalable pretraining strategy enables CLIP to learn transferable visual representations and perform zero-shot recognition by comparing image features with natural language prompts. Due to its strong image-text alignment ability, CLIP has been widely adopted as a general-purpose backbone for many downstream tasks, including zero-shot and few-shot image classification, test-time adaptation, robust recognition, anomaly detection, image-language understanding, visual question answering, and compositional zero-shot learning ( Martin et al., 2024 ; Saha et al., 2024 ; Zanella and Ben Ayed, 2024 ; Ge et al., 2023 ; An et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2026 ; Jeong et al., 2023 ; Tschannen et al., 2023 ; Guo et al., 2023 ; Chen and Wu, 2024 ; Lu et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) . These studies demonstrate the broad transferability of pretrained vision-language representations. At the same time, they also suggest that the way a task is formulated in language can strongly affect how CLIP is used. This issue is particularly relevant to CIR, where the query text often specifies how one visual state should be transformed into another rather than simply describing a static image. In composed image retrieval, CLIP is particularly attractive because the task naturally requires matching visual content with language descriptions. Existing ZS-CIR methods often reuse CLIP as the core retrieval backbone, either by mapping the reference image into a pseudo-word token, generating target captions, or composing reference and modification semantics in the CLIP feature space ( Saito et al., 2023 ; Baldrati et al., 2023 ; Karthik et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) . Their success nevertheless depends on the ability of the pretrained text encoder to represent transformation-oriented language in a form suitable for matching completed visual states. This issue is relevant to negation, counting, relational changes, and object removal, where a query may mention concepts or attributes that should not appear in the target. In this work, we retain CLIP as the retrieval backbone but study whether reformulating the query as observable target-state semantics provides a more suitable retrieval representation under a controlled CIR protocol. 3 Method This section presents ASAP-CIR as a concrete training-free solution to the query representation problem in zero-shot composed image retrieval (ZS-CIR). We use dynamic semantics to denote instructions that specify a transition from the reference state, and target-state semantics to denote visually observable content in the desired result. Motivated by the controlled evidence in Sec. 4.3 , ASAP-CIR follows a representation-centered pipeline: it reconstructs the intended target state from the composed query, expresses that state through complementary holistic descriptions and importance-weighted atomic semantics, and grounds both levels against candidate images. CLIP is therefore used primarily to align observable target-state semantics rather than to infer the transformation itself. Figure 2: Overview of the proposed ASAP-CIR framework. First, the generated text should describe the final target image directly, rather than explaining the editing process from the reference image. Second, each atomic semantic should correspond to a visually observable static fact, such as an object, attribute, relation, material, count, style, or scene cue. In other words, expressions such as “remove the dog” or “change the bottle to orange” are discouraged, while static formulations such as “a single dog is visible” or “an orange soft drink bottle is present” are preferred. This explicit constraint is important because it aligns the generated text with the static image-caption form on which CLIP-like models are pretrained. We use dataset-specific prompts because the preservation assumptions are different across benchmarks. In FashionIQ, the reference garment usually provides important identity and style information, so unchanged garment attributes should be retained unless they conflict with the modification. In CIRR and CIRCO, the modification may explicitly add, remove, or replace objects and scene context, so the MLLM is asked to infer which reference details should remain visible and which should be suppressed. Following recent ZS-CIR studies ( Lim et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) , we evaluate ASAP-CIR on three widely used composed image retrieval benchmarks: FashionIQ ( Wu et al., 2021 ) , CIRR ( Liu et al., 2021 ) , and CIRCO ( Baldrati et al., 2023 ) . FashionIQ is a fashion-domain retrieval benchmark containing three categories, namely Dress, Shirt, and Toptee. We evaluate on the validation split and report recall at rank k k (R@ k k ), with k ∈ { 10 , 50 } k\in\{10,50\} , for each category, together with their average over the three categories. CIRR is an open-domain benchmark constructed from real-life images sourced from NLVR2. It augments reference–target image pairs with human-written relative captions that describe the intended semantic change, thereby emphasizing fine-grained discrimination among visually similar natural images. CIRR provides both full-gallery and visually restricted subset evaluation protocols. We evaluate on the test1 split and report full-gallery R@ k k with k ∈ { 1 , 5 , 10 , 50 } k\in\{1,5,10,50\} ; to keep the main comparison focused on this setting, we do not report subset recall. CIRCO is built from the COCO 2017 unlabeled image set and provides multiple ground-truth target images for each query. It contains 123,403 candidate images and 800 test queries. Following the official evaluation protocol, we report mean average precision at rank k k (mAP@ k k ), with k ∈ { 5 , 10 , 25 , 50 } k\in\{5,10,25,50\} . Baselines. We compare ASAP-CIR with representative zero-shot composed image retrieval methods using reported backbone architecture groups whenever available. The compared methods include training-based or language-supervised approaches, such as Pic2Word ( Saito et al., 2023 ) , SEARLE ( Baldrati et al., 2023 ) , LinCIR ( Gu et al., 2024 ) , FlowCIR ( He et al., 2026 ) , DiffComp ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , and TT-RLDR ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) . We also compare with recent training-free methods that rely on foundation models or test-time reasoning, including CIReVL ( Karthik et al., 2024 ) , LDRE ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , AutoCIR ( Cheng et al., 2025 ) , OSrCIR ( Tang et al., 2025 ) , and STiTch ( Li et al., 2026 ) . In the tables, T-Free denotes whether a method is training-free. We group methods by their reported visual encoder architecture for readability, while noting that exact pretrained checkpoints, preprocessing pipelines, and implementation details may differ across papers. Following common practice, the best and second-best results within each backbone group are shown in bold and underlined , respectively. Implementation Details. ASAP-CIR is a training-free method and does not use any CIR triplets for optimization. We use Qwen3.6-27B as the frozen MLLM for static semantic parsing of queries. In our implementation, the number of holistic descriptions is controlled by the hyperparameter num-target-descriptions , and we set K = 3 K=3 by default. If fewer than K K valid descriptions are produced, the last valid description is repeated until the number reaches K K ; if more than K K descriptions are produced, only the first K K descriptions are retained.
